name: Amira Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm the office administrator at Harlow & Sons, a family funeral firm with three branches, and I sit in the head office on Station Road. I start at half eight with the overnight messages, because people often ring the out-of-hours line when someone dies at home. Then it's the diary: booking the chapel, the crematorium slots, the cars, the celebrants and the florists, and making sure nothing double-books.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the rest of the day look like after the diary?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paperwork, mostly. Every funeral has a file: the death certificate copy, the cremation forms, the invoices, the family's choices for music and flowers. I keep all of that straight and chase the doctors' surgeries when a form is late. Denise, who's worked here twenty years, does the accounts side, and I do everything else in the office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. If I get a date wrong, a family stands in the rain waiting for a hearse that isn't coming, so I'm careful, and I'm proud of being careful. What wears me out is the phone on a bad week, and the crematorium's booking website, which logs you out every ten minutes. Graham Harlow, the owner, still prints every email, so I file things twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of the gadgets we've been sold. My boss Graham bought a scanner that was meant to make us paperless, and now we have a scanner and paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says about most new things: let's see it work first. At work I'd probably joke that the crematorium website still can't keep me logged in, so I'm not too worried about it running my diary. Online I don't really post about work, given what we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. I earn more than most administrators round here because Graham trusts me with the families, and I've got about nine months of pay saved. If AI only tidies up the typing, my job stays my job and I keep my plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the same, and maybe let the new transcription tool write up the arrangement notes so I'm not typing after six. I'd keep putting 600 a month into the house fund that Emre, my fiancé, and I share. The wedding is booked for next June, so that money doesn't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because everyone has been told this is the big thing. But calm is good for me; I like a steady year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the wedding and the house fund. What's the biggest money pressure on you right now, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, if I'm honest. Emre's family and mine are both big, so we're at 180 guests, and my mother has opinions about every table. But it's paid for in stages, and we planned it so the house fund isn't touched. Nothing in this picture changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd watch out for, even in this quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise, a little. Denise does the accounts on an old system and she hates every update. If the accounts software starts doing half her checking, I think Graham would ask whether he needs her five days a week. I'd hate that, because Denise taught me everything.

say: I'd say **show me it working** before anyone gets excited about AI in our office.
I'd joke that the **crematorium website** can't even keep me logged in, so it won't run my diary.
think: Privately I'd be **relieved**, because my pay, my savings and my plans stay as they are.
My worth to Graham is **trust with families**, and typing help doesn't touch that.
do: Use the **transcription tool** for arrangement notes so I stop typing after six.
Keep paying **600 a month** into the house fund I share with Emre.
Leave the **wedding budget** for next June exactly as planned.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a little flatness after all the big promises about AI.
S0.quote: My boss Graham bought a scanner that was meant to make us paperless, and now we have a scanner and paper.
fieldNote: She measures new technology against **proof in the office**, echoing her father's habit of waiting to see it work.
Her security rests on **trust with grieving families**, which she sees as the part software can't touch.
Even in the calm picture she quietly **worries for Denise**, the older colleague on the accounts side.

steps.text: Keep running the funeral diary and files exactly as now
Pay 600 a month into the shared house fund
Let the transcription tool type up arrangement notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking, checking, answering customers. That's my job description read back to me, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we're a family firm and families want a person, which is true and which Graham likes hearing. To friends I'd say it's sensible to learn the new systems before they're forced on you. I wouldn't say I was scared, because I don't like making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the second desk goes. If a system books the chapel, the cars and the crematorium on its own and chases the forms, Graham doesn't need two of us in the office. Denise has the seniority, but I have the computer skills, so I honestly don't know which of us he'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham straight out if I can sit in on arrangement meetings with families, because that's the part no booking system does. I'd do the funeral arranger certificate that the trade association runs, about 900 and evenings for six months. And I'd stop topping up the wedding extras, the band and the second photographer, until I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I don't panic, but I'd lie awake doing the sums, which is what I do when something's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't like making a fuss. Would you tell Emre you were worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Emre, yes, but in my own way, at the kitchen table with the numbers in front of us. Emre is an electrician, so his work isn't going anywhere. My fiancé Emre would say we'll be fine on his wage, and that's kind, but I didn't study for two years to be kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for a shift like that, if anyone is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Graham; he's running a business, and if the software is cheaper he has to look at it. I'd look more at the big tech firms selling it as magic and the colleges still teaching people filing as if it's 2005. People should be pushed towards skills with a future while they're young, like an apprenticeship.

say: At work I'd say **families want a person**, which is true and pleases Graham.
To friends I'd say learn the **new systems** before they're forced on you.
think: I think the **second desk goes** once software books the chapel, cars and crematorium.
I honestly don't know whether Graham keeps **Denise or me**, and that unsettles me.
do: Ask Graham to let me **sit in** on arrangement meetings with families.
Take the **funeral arranger certificate**, about 900 and six months of evenings.
Pause the **wedding extras** like the band and second photographer until things settle.
feel: **Unsettled** rather than panicked, lying awake doing the sums at night.
S1.quote: My fiancé Emre would say we'll be fine on his wage, and that's kind, but I didn't study for two years to be kept.
fieldNote: She reads the card as her **own job description**, which sharpens the threat straight away.
Her plan moves her towards the **families' side** of the business, the part she sees as human.
Pride in **earning her own way** runs alongside her traditional views on family and marriage.
She blames **tech sellers and colleges**, not her employer, for leaving workers unprepared.

steps.text: Ask Graham for a seat in family arrangement meetings
Take the trade association's funeral arranger certificate over six months
Drop the wedding band and second photographer for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding photos are even printed, near enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say something calm, because the families need us calm, and Graham would want a steady face. To friends I'd say the people pushing this haven't thought about ordinary families at all. I might even share something online about it, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I think my office job is finished by 2028. Every part of my day is thinking work: the diary, the forms, the chasing, the invoices, and the card says AI does all of that better and cheaper. The hands-on side of a funeral, the carrying and the dressing and the driving, lasts until robots come around 2031, but that's not the side I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask Graham to train me on the arranging and the funeral home side, even the hands-on care of the deceased, because that buys me three more years. I'd move the house money from the deposit plan into an easy-access account so it's ready if I'm out of work. And Emre and I would talk about doing a smaller wedding and keeping the difference, maybe 8,000 back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly, under the calm face. I'd hold it together at work and then cry in the car park, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move into the hands-on side for three more years. Would that be enough time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not on its own, no. Three years buys me time to build up savings and see what's left, but if robots can carry a coffin and families accept that, then I'm out again. What I'm really betting on is that families in our town won't accept a robot at a graveside, and I could be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a smaller wedding. What would your mother say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would be upset at first, because the big wedding is for the family as much as for us. But she lived through hard times when I was little, and she'd understand keeping money aside. I'd tell my mother it's the marriage that matters, not the 180 chairs.

say: At work I'd keep a **steady face**, because grieving families need us calm.
To friends I'd say the people pushing this **forgot ordinary families** completely.
think: I think my **office job ends** by 2028, because every part of it is thinking work.
The **hands-on side** of funerals lasts until about 2031, but that isn't my side yet.
do: Ask Graham to train me in **arranging and care** of the deceased within a month.
Move the house money into an **easy-access account** in case I lose work.
Cut the wedding down with Emre and keep about **8,000 back**.
feel: **Frightened** underneath, holding it together at work and crying in the car park.
Some **stubborn hope** that families in her town will refuse robots at gravesides.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mother it's the marriage that matters, not the 180 chairs.
fieldNote: She sees the **robot gap** as only three more years, not a real escape.
Her real bet is on **local custom**: families refusing machines at a graveside.
The scenario pushes her to **shrink the wedding**, a big step against family expectations.

steps.text: Train in arranging and hands-on care of the deceased this month
Move the house deposit into an easy-access savings account
Shrink the June wedding and keep about 8,000 back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Not good, but I could breathe a bit in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said with the slow one: families want a person, and firms like ours should keep people where it counts. I'd say it more firmly, though, because I'd have time to show I meant it. Online, I'd probably still keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my desk job still goes, just around 2031 instead of 2028. But five years is enough to become a qualified funeral arranger and maybe a funeral director, which is half talking to families and half hands-on, and the hands-on half has until about 2034. That's a proper plan, not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the arranger certificate this year and then the director's diploma, about 2,500 all in, which I can pay from savings. I'd keep the wedding as booked and keep the house fund going, because we'd have time to buy before anything breaks. And I'd ask Graham whether Harlow & Sons would ever let me buy into a branch one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a working way. Like before a big funeral, when you know the list is long but you've got the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about buying into a branch. Is that realistic for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a long shot, and Graham has sons, which is in the name. But one son is in banking and the other has no interest, and Graham has said more than once he worries who carries it on. With savings and Emre's wage, a small share in the Millbrook branch isn't mad in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting out in office work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Aylin, who's just turned 18, not to do the office diploma I did. I'd tell her to get a trade or a skill where people want a person in the room, and to learn the AI tools on the side so she isn't scared of them. Apprenticeships over another desk course, every time.

say: I'd say firmly that firms like ours should keep **people where it counts**.
Online I'd still **keep quiet**, because I don't post about work.
think: My **desk job** still goes, just around 2031 instead of 2028.
Five years is enough to qualify as a **funeral director**, half families and half hands-on.
do: Start the arranger certificate, then the **director's diploma**, about 2,500 from savings.
Keep the **wedding as booked** and keep the house fund going.
Ask Graham about one day **buying into** the Millbrook branch.
feel: **Nervous** in a working way, like facing a long list before a big funeral.
S3.quote: I'd tell my cousin Aylin, who's just turned 18, not to do the office diploma I did.
fieldNote: Five years turns a scramble into a **staged plan**: certificate, diploma, then perhaps ownership.
Her ambition to **buy into a branch** surfaced only once she had time to think.
She'd steer younger relatives to **apprenticeships**, in line with her traditional views on work.

steps.text: Start the funeral arranger certificate this year, then the director's diploma
Ask Graham about buying a share in the Millbrook branch
Keep paying into the house fund alongside the booked wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole other life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, and that families and firms should use it instead of pretending it isn't coming. I'd probably say it at church too, because a lot of the older people there are frightened by the news. I'd want to sound sensible, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's the version I can handle. My office work still goes by 2036, but by then I'd want to be a funeral director, ideally with a share in a branch, and the robots for the hands-on side wouldn't be good enough until about 2039. That's most of my working thirties covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same courses as in the five-year one, just without rushing, and use the AI tools at work now so I understand what's coming. We'd buy the house in the next two years as planned, maybe start a family around 30. And I'd keep saving the 600 a month, because ten years of that is a real cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not frightened like the two-year one, more like knowing winter's coming and getting the coal in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned starting a family around 30. Would this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the plan itself, no. Children are the point of all of it for me, and I wouldn't let a computer decide that. It might change what I tell our children to study, though, more than anything about when we have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a gap between what you'd tell people at church and what you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. At church I'd say we have time and we should be sensible, and I'd mean it. But privately I know ten years goes quickly, and I've watched Graham say 'next year' about the same new software for five years running.

say: I'd say we have **time to prepare** properly, so families and firms shouldn't pretend.
At **church** I'd sound sensible rather than scary for the older people.
think: My office work still goes by 2036, but I'd hope to be a **funeral director** by then.
Robots for hands-on work arriving around **2039** covers most of my working thirties.
do: Take the arranger and director courses at a **steady pace** over several years.
Use **AI tools at work** now so I understand what's coming.
Buy the **house** within two years and keep saving 600 a month.
feel: **Uneasy**, like knowing winter is coming and getting the supplies in early.
S4.quote: Children are the point of all of it for me, and I wouldn't let a computer decide that.
fieldNote: The decade lets her keep **family plans intact**, which matters more to her than career.
She admits a gap: calm at **church**, privately aware that ten years passes fast.
She doubts Graham's pace, having heard **'next year'** about software for five years.

steps.text: Take the arranger and director courses at a steady pace
Use the firm's AI booking tools now to learn them
Keep saving 600 a month into a family cushion
Buy a house with Emre within the next two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it lands right on the wedding and the house and there's no time to retrain. What would help is firms like ours being told early and clearly, so Graham could plan who moves where instead of just cutting. And proper apprenticeships for people my age, paid ones, into work that needs a person, like arranging or care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the families think. Nobody asks them, and they're the ones who'll decide if a machine is allowed at a funeral. I've sat with a grieving woman who held my hand while picking the hymns. No booking system holds your hand.

headlineQuote: I've sat with a grieving woman who held my hand while picking the hymns. No booking system holds your hand.
portrait: Amira, 27, runs the office at **Harlow & Sons**, a three-branch family funeral firm, and prides herself on care.
She's engaged to Emre, an electrician, with a **June wedding** booked and about nine months of pay saved.
She waits for **proof** before trusting new technology and stays calm while AI only nibbles at routine tasks.
Faster AGI pushes her towards the **families' side** of funerals, where she believes people still want a person.
The two-year picture **alarms** her most, while ten years lets her plan courses, a house and children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because it lands on the wedding and house with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **early warning** to small firms, so owners like Graham can move people instead of cutting.
Paid **apprenticeships** for people her age into work that needs a person, like arranging or care.
